displayQuote: My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me

meta.title: Who really said "My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Henry Ford. Wikiquote traces this friendship line to a May 1914 saying by California reformer Harris Weinstock, misattributed to Ford by 1948.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Henry Ford. It is a modern trimming of a 1914 line by Harris Weinstock, pinned on Ford by 1948 with no primary source.

answer.label: Not Henry Ford — actually Harris Weinstock
answer.sourceLine: There is no speech, book, letter, or interview in which Henry Ford said this. Wikiquote’s Misattributed section ↗ traces the thought to Harris Weinstock, who in May 1914 said, “My best friend is the man who can bring out of me my best, and your best friend is the one who tends to bring out the best in you.” The familiar one-line Ford version is a later trimming of Weinstock’s words, first attached to Ford only as late as 1948.

source.heading: Where it really comes from
source.excerpt: My best friend is the man who can bring out of me my best, and your best friend is the one who tends to bring out the best in you.
trail: The line appears on Goodreads ↗ and dozens of quote-aggregator pages credited to Henry Ford, always without a source.
Wikiquote ↗ files it under Misattributed, correcting it to Harris Weinstock’s longer May 1914 saying and noting the Ford credit is documented only “as early as 1948.”
Harris Weinstock (1854–1922) was a Sacramento merchant and California’s first State Market Commissioner who sat on President Wilson’s U.S. Commission on Industrial Relations, per Wikipedia ↗.
source.excerptNote: Harris Weinstock’s May 1914 wording, as recorded in Wikiquote ↗. The popular “My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me” is a compressed rewrite of this longer original.
source.rightsNote: Harris Weinstock’s original statement dates to May 1914 and is therefore in the U.S. public domain (first published well before 1931). The clipped Ford-style wording is an unattributed modern paraphrase of that public-domain line, so no one holds rights to it.

author.name: Harris Weinstock
author.heading: Who was Harris Weinstock?
author.bio: Harris Weinstock (1854–1922) was a London-born, California-raised merchant who co-founded the Sacramento department store that became Weinstock’s. A civic reformer, he served as California’s first State Market Commissioner and, from 1913, on President Woodrow Wilson’s U.S. Commission on Industrial Relations. His May 1914 remark about friends who “bring out the best” in one another is the documented root of the line later miscredited to Henry Ford.

misattribution.heading: How Ford got the credit
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook celebrity-magnet misquote: a warm, quotable line drifts off its little-known author and lands on a household name.

items.why: Credited to Ford across Goodreads ↗ and countless quote sites with no speech, book, or letter behind it. Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Misattributed and dates the Ford credit no earlier than 1948.

Weinstock’s longer May 1914 line — “My best friend is the man who can bring out of me my best, and your best friend is the one who tends to bring out the best in you” — is the wording Wikiquote ↗ identifies as the source of the trimmed Ford quote.

misattribution.truthLine: The one-sentence “Henry Ford” quote is a modern compression of Harris Weinstock’s May 1914 remark; per Wikiquote ↗ the attribution to Ford appears only by 1948.

context.heading: Why the mix-up sticks
lead: Friendship maxims are among the most-forwarded quotes online, and they reliably migrate to the most famous name in reach. Henry Ford — endlessly quoted for “Whether you think you can or you can’t, you’re right” — is a natural magnet, so a stray line about friends who “bring out the best” in us settled on him rather than on a Sacramento merchant few readers would recognize.

Harris Weinstock’s original was a balanced two-part observation about mutual improvement between friends. Stripped to a single clause and set in the first person, it became the tidy, greeting-card “Ford” line that circulates today.
context.pull: A warm line drifts off its little-known author and lands on a household name.
